label: Ductal_Carcinoma_In_Situ_DCIS
answer_markdown:
## Key Facts

- Neoplastic epithelial proliferation confined to mammary ducts/lobules without stromal invasion
- Mammographically detected primarily via microcalcifications (70–80%)
- Wide spectrum of nuclear grades and architectural patterns; comedo necrosis seen in high-grade lesions
- Risk factor for subsequent invasive carcinoma; not all cases progress
- Intact myoepithelial cell layer distinguishes DCIS from invasive carcinoma
- ER is the only routinely recommended biomarker for DCIS; PR is optional

## Terminology

- Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)
- Synonyms: Intraductal carcinoma
- Not recommended: "Ductal intraepithelial neoplasia," "mammary intraepithelial neoplasia" ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html))
- "Extensive DCIS" used only when >25% of an invasive carcinoma area is DCIS or DCIS extends beyond the invasive into surrounding tissue

## Essential and Desirable Diagnostic Criteria

- **Essential:**
  - Malignant, clonal proliferation of epithelial cells entirely confined within the basement membrane-bound ducts/lobules ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html); [Breast Atlas, p.235](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=235))
  - No evidence of invasion into surrounding stroma; myoepithelial cell layer intact ([Breast Biopsy, p.291](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Biopsy.pdf#page=291))
  - Defines by: Cytological atypia (mild to severe), variable architectural growth patterns (comedo, cribriform, micropapillary, solid, papillary) ([Breast Atlas, p.235](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=235))
  - Present in both women and men (rare in men)
- **Desirable:**
  - Immunohistochemical staining for ER (routine), PR (optional) ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html); [Breast Atlas, p.244](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=244))
  - E-cadherin positivity supports ductal (vs. lobular) differentiation ([Breast Atlas, p.315](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=315))
  - Oncotype DX DCIS genomic testing (if used) ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html))

## Etiology/Pathogenesis

- Risk factors overlap with invasive breast cancer: age, family history, nulliparity, late menopause, high breast density, hormone therapy, BRCA1/2 ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html))
- Represents early nonobligate precursor to invasive carcinoma
- Molecularly heterogeneous; high-grade DCIS shares mutations with associated invasive carcinoma (PIK3CA, TP53, GATA3); HER2 amplified in ~30% ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/BREAST/Carcinoma_In_Situ.html); [PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/stainsbreasther2.html))
- Germline BRCA1/2 mutations in 3.3–5.9% of women with DCIS ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html))

## Clinical Issues

- **Epidemiology:**
  - Represents 20–25% of newly diagnosed breast cancers in the US ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html))
  - Mean age: 50–59 years; rare under age 30; more common with increasing age ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html))
- **Presentation:**
  - Most commonly non-palpable, discovered as microcalcifications on screening mammogram (70–80%)
  - Less commonly as palpable mass, nipple discharge, or Paget disease ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html))
  - Can occur in axillary breast tissue
- **Natural History:**
  - Increased risk (2–8.6x) of invasive carcinoma versus general population
  - Not all DCIS progresses; 36–53% of low-grade DCIS untreated may develop invasion ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html))
- **Treatment:**
  - Surgical excision with negative margins; breast-conserving surgery ± radiation ([Breast Pattern, p.167](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Pattern.pdf#page=167)), sometimes mastectomy
  - ER+ cases may receive adjuvant hormonal therapy
- **Prognosis:** Generally excellent with complete excision ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/BREAST/Carcinoma_In_Situ.html))

## Macroscopic

- No consistent gross findings; often not visible/palpable
- May appear as ill-defined or granular indurated area if large
- Microcalcifications may be palpable as grittiness ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html))

## Microscopic

- Proliferation of malignant epithelial cells filling and expanding ducts/lobules
- **Growth patterns:**
  - Solid: ducts completely filled by neoplastic cells ([Breast Atlas, p.236](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=236))
  - Cribriform: round, punched-out spaces within proliferating cells
  - Micropapillary: delicate, slender fibrovascular projections into lumen
  - Papillary: true fibrovascular cores
  - Comedo: central necrosis, often with calcification ([Breast Atlas, p.239](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=239))
- **Nuclear grade:**
  - Low-grade: small, uniform nuclei; limited mitoses ([Breast Atlas, p.236](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=236))
  - High-grade: large, pleomorphic nuclei; frequent mitoses, necrosis ([Breast Atlas, p.239](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=239))
- **Other features:**
  - Intact myoepithelial cell layer
  - May involve sclerosing adenosis, raising suspicion for microinvasion — special stains confirm in situ nature ([Breast Biopsy, p.291](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Biopsy.pdf#page=291))
  - Variants: apocrine, clear cell, spindle cell, cystic hypersecretory, small cell, adenoid cystic ([Breast Atlas, p.241](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=241))

![Low grade, cribriform DCIS](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/breastmalignantDCISTozbikian03.jpg)
![High-grade DCIS with comedo necrosis](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-public-figures-830130787988/textbook_figures_web_v1/breast_atlas/breast_atlas_p0240_fig01_fig_11_11.jpeg)
![DCIS, solid type with microcalcifications](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/caseofweek/Case533img2.jpg)

## Cytology

- FNA: neoplastic cells present as single or sheets with eccentric, atypical nuclei; background may contain necrotic debris or calcification ([Breast Atlas, p.438](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=438))

## Ancillary Tests

- **Immunohistochemistry:**
  - ER: positive in 75–80% of cases (range <1–100%); high-grade may be ER/PR negative ([Breast Atlas, p.244](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=244); [PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html))
  - PR: expression somewhat lower; optional for routine use
  - HER2: overexpressed in ~30% (especially high-grade)
  - E-cadherin: positive (helps distinguish from LCIS, where negative) ([Breast Atlas, p.315](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=315))
  - Myoepithelial cell markers (p63, smooth muscle myosin) demonstrate intact peripheral myoepithelial layer ([Breast Atlas, p.322](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=322))
  - Basaloid DCIS: negative for ER/PR/HER2, positive for CK5/6, CK14, CK17, vimentin, EGFR ([Breast Pattern, p.167](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Pattern.pdf#page=167))
- **Genetic/Molecular:**
  - Oncotype DX for DCIS risk stratification ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html))

## Radiology

- Mammography: microcalcifications in 72–98% of cases ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html)), often the only finding
- Less often, mass or architectural distortion (may be higher grade or advanced cases)
- Pleomorphic calcifications suggest high-grade; fine/granular with low-grade
- Ultrasound: limited sensitivity for DCIS
- MRI: useful adjunct where DCIS lacks calcifications, for mapping multifocal/multicentric disease ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html))
![Mammogram: DCIS presenting as microcalcifications](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/caseofweek/Case533img1.jpg)

## Differential Diagnosis

- **Usual ductal hyperplasia (UDH):** 
  - Polyclonal, polymorphic cells with streaming/irregular bridging; lacks cytologic atypia, lacks rigid secondary spaces
  - No nucleomegaly or overt hyperchromasia ([Breast Atlas, p.235](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=235))
- **Atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH):**
  - Shares cytology/architecture with low-grade DCIS but <2mm or <2 contiguous spaces involved; intermediate risk ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastadh.html))
- **LCIS (classic/pleomorphic/florid):**
  - Negative for E-cadherin (vs. positive in DCIS); small, uniform, discohesive cells; lack of intraductal bridging ([Breast Atlas, p.315](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Atlas.pdf#page=315); [PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantlcis.html))
- **Collagenous spherulosis:**
  - Presents as spherules of basement membrane material surrounded by bland epithelium and myoepithelial cells ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html))
- **Papilloma/atypical papilloma:**
  - Contains both epithelial and myoepithelial cells, prominent fibrous stroma/core, haphazard cell orientation, apocrine metaplasia present ([Breast Biopsy, p.255](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Biopsy.pdf#page=255))
- **Encapsulated papillary carcinoma/solid papillary carcinoma:**
  - Lack myoepithelium around tumor or papillae; more circumscribed architecture ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantencapsulatedpapillary.html))

## Prognostic Factors

- Positive surgical margins increase recurrence risk ([PathOutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/breastmalignantDCIS.html))
- High nuclear grade, large lesion size, comedo necrosis, and patient age <45 years correlate with higher risk of recurrence
- ER negativity associated with increased ipsilateral recurrence
- Local recurrence rates after breast-conserving therapy: up to 40% at 15 years, with 28% as invasive cancer
- Time to recurrence: >15 years for low-grade versus <5 years for high-grade lesions

## Illustrative Cases

- DCIS involving sclerosing adenosis may mimic microinvasion; smooth muscle myosin immunostaining confirms intact myoepithelial cells ([Breast Biopsy, p.291](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Biopsy.pdf#page=291))
- DCIS and LCIS may co-occur in the same involved spaces ([Breast Biopsy, p.114](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/Breast_Biopsy.pdf#page=114))

The neoplastic cells have basally located nuclei and contain abundant intracytoplasmic mucin. Mucin is also present within the cystic spaces. The degree of cytological atypia is variable, even within the same tumour. The cystic structures have a rounded contour but lack myoepithelial cells at the periphery. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) may be present in the adjacent mammary ducts and lobules. Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma should be differentiated from pure mucinous carcinoma (see section Mucinous carcinoma) and encapsulated papillary carcinoma (see section Encapsulated papillary carcinoma), both of which are typically strongly and diffusely positive for ER and PR. cards.excerpt: Entity: Carcinoma in situ Section: pathogenesis The etiological factors are similar to those of invasive carcinoma of the female breast and are discussed in section that section . --- The pathogenesis is similar to that of invasive male breast carcinoma (see section Invasive carcinoma). Data on the molecular profile of male carcinoma in situ, which are scant and concern DCIS, point towards a close relationship between in situ and associated invasive carcinoma, with similar mutations in PIK3CA, TP53, and GATA3 and copy-number aberrations for common oncogenes. In rare cases, columnar cell–like changes present adjacent to DCIS, and invasive carcinoma showed the same mutation profile. X chromosome aneusomy associated with AR copy-number gain has been identified in DCIS.

cards.title: Carcinoma in situ
cards.excerpt: Entity: Carcinoma in situ Section: prognosis_and_prediction Carcinoma in situ associated with invasive carcinoma is treated similarly to invasive disease. For pure DCIS, the prognosis is good. In one series, 4 of 31 cases recurred: 1 case as DCIS and 3 cases as invasive carcinoma. It has been suggested that the presence of DCIS next to invasive carcinoma is associated with longer overall survival in the luminal A and luminal B HER2-enriched groups.

cards.excerpt: Entity: Carcinoma in situ Section: microscopic Although the entire spectrum of carcinoma in situ observed in the female breast can also be found in the male breast, the vast majority (97.9%) of male carcinoma in situ is DCIS, whereas lobular carcinoma in situ is rare. Most pure DCIS is of low or intermediate nuclear grade and of papillary or micropapillary architecture, whereas high-grade DCIS with comedonecrosis is usually associated with high-grade invasive carcinoma. The nuclear grade, histotype, and immunophenotype of DCIS usually correlate with the grade and type of associated invasive carcinoma. cards.excerpt: Entity: Carcinoma in situ Section: clinical Carcinoma in situ of the male breast presents in three different clinical settings: as an occasional finding in gynaecomastia, in association with invasive carcinoma, or as pure carcinoma in situ with variable symptoms and clinical features. Symptom duration ranges from a few months to 8 years. Pure carcinoma in situ most often presents as a retroareolar mass affecting elderly men, with a mean age range of 58–65 years, and it can be bilateral. Rarely, carcinoma in situ can affect young men and adolescents. Large duct involvement is associated with bloody nipple discharge. In Paget disease, there is an enlarging eczematous lesion of the nipple–areola complex. Diagnosis by mammography alone can be difficult, and MRI can be helpful in reaching the correct diagnosis. --- Male carcinoma in situ, which is almost exclusively ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), is associated with invasive carcinoma in as many as 46.2% of cases. cards.title: DCIS — Intraductal carcinoma
cards.excerpt:
Ductal intraepithelial neoplasia: terminology never widely adopted and removed from the 4th Edition WHO classification of mammary neoplasms (International Agency for Research on Cancer: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Breast, 4th Edition, 2012)
Mammary intraepithelial neoplasia: a general term to include both ductal and lobular intraepithelial neoplasia but never adopted, terminology should not be used (Am J Surg Pathol 1991;15:209, Hum Pathol 2002;33:620, Am J Surg Pathol 1980;4:241)
Extensive DCIS / extensive intraductal component: terminology should only be used to describe DCIS that is associated with invasive carcinoma in which the DCIS component constitutes > 25% of the entire area of invasive carcinoma and DCIS extends beyond the invasive carcinoma into the surrounding breast tissue (Pathol Annu 1988;23:1)
Multicentric DCIS: no uniform definition, generally refers to DCIS that involves multiple breast quadrants and different distinct regions of the breast

cards.title: DCIS — Epidemiology
cards.excerpt:
Similar epidemiologic risk factors to invasive breast cancer, including older age, family history of breast cancer, nulliparity, late age at first birth, late menopause, elevated body mass index, high mammographic breast density, postmenopausal hormonal therapy use and genetic risk factors (e.g. BRCA1/2) (Mol Oncol 2010;4:357, Clinics (Sao Paulo) 2013;68:674, J Transl Med 2015;13:335)
Incidence of DCIS increased significantly from 1983 - 1992 due to greater mammographic screening, particularly in patients younger than 50 years old (JAMA 1996;275:913, J Natl Cancer Inst Monogr 1997:151)
Represents 20 - 25% of newly diagnosed breast cancers in the United States (CA Cancer J Clin 2017;67:7, Am Surg 2018;84:1)
3.3 - 5.9% of women with DCIS carry a germline mutation in BRCA1 or BRCA2 and prevalence of BRCA mutation is significantly greater in women diagnosed with DCIS before the age 50 and personal or family history of breast cancer (JAMA 2005;293:964, Cancer Prev Res (Phila) 2010;3:1579, J Clin Oncol 2002;20:1480)

cards.title: DCIS — MRI of a linear enhancementPrognostic factors
cards.excerpt:
Women diagnosed with DCIS have 10 times higher risk of developing ipsilateral invasive breast if untreated (N Engl J Med 2004;350:1430, Cancer 1982;49:751)
36 - 53% of low grade DCIS lesions progress to invasive lesions if untreated (Mod Pathol 2015;28:662, Cancer 1980;46:919)
Risk of progression of untreated high grade DCIS to invasive carcinoma is not well characterized as most clinically detected high grade DCIS is excised surgically (N Engl J Med 2004;350:1430)
Time interval to the development of recurrence varies, low grade DCIS has longer interval (> 15 years), shorter interval observed in high grade DCIS (< 5 years) (Cancer 2005;103:1778)
Long term outcome meta analysis study of DCIS showed a 15 year total local recurrence rate of 40% with 28% recurring as invasive disease (BMC Cancer 2015;15:890)
Positive surgical margins, high nuclear grade, large lesion size, comedo necrosis and young age (< 45 years) reported as the most important clinical pathologic predictors associated with local recurrence and prognosis (J Clin Oncol 1996;14:754, Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys 2001;50:991, Cancer 1999;85:616, J Clin Oncol 2006;24:3381, Cancer 2005;103:2481, Breast Cancer Res Treat 2008;109:405, Eur J Cancer 2007;43:291, Breast J 2005;11:242)
A nomogram for predicting recurrence risk after breast conserving surgery based on clinical, pathologic and treatment variables has shown utility in providing individualized estimates of recurrence risk (J Clin Oncol 2010;28:3762)

cards.title: DCIS — Predictive and prognostic biomarkers and ancillary testing in DCIS
cards.excerpt:
Estrogen receptor
Currently the only immunohistochemical biomarker recommended for routine clinical use; progesterone receptor is considered optional (J Clin Oncol 2020:JCO1902309)
Determines potential benefit of endocrine therapies (J Clin Oncol 2020:JCO1902309, Lancet 1999;353:1993)
ER negative status correlates with ipsilateral recurrence risk (Breast Cancer Res Treat 2018;167:751)
Oncotype DX for DCIS® assay is a genomic test that predicts radiation therapy benefit and the likelihood of 10 year breast cancer local recurrence risk in patients with DCIS treated with breast conserving surgery (J Natl Cancer Inst 2013;105:701, Breast Cancer Res Treat 2015;152:389, J Natl Cancer Inst 2017;109)

cards.excerpt:

cards.title: DCIS — Treatment
cards.excerpt:
Breast conserving surgery alone, breast conserving surgery with radiotherapy or mastectomy
Excision to negative margins (≥ 2 mm) for patients treated with breast conserving surgery (Pract Radiat Oncol 2016;6:287)
Possible sentinel lymph node sampling if patients are planned for mastectomy or who have DCIS size > 5 cm or at high risk of microinvasive carcinoma (Ann Surg Oncol 2016;23:2229, Am J Surg 2008;196:81, Breast J 2008;14:135)
Radiation reduces the risk of local recurrence by 50% in patients undergoing breast conserving therapy (J Clin Oncol 2008;26:1247)
Tamoxifen therapy further decreases the risk of ipsilateral and contralateral recurrence by 30% in patients with estrogen receptor positive DCIS (Semin Oncol 2006;33:647, Breast Cancer Res Treat 2002;75:S7)
Aromatase inhibitors with similar overall effectiveness to tamoxifen, with different safety profile (Lancet 2016;387:866, Lancet 2016;387:857)
Omission of radiotherapy may be considered if DCIS is small, low grade and has clear margins (J Clin Oncol 2009;27:3211)
Mastectomy may be recommended for multicentric DCIS, inability to attain clear surgical margins, large span or diffuse microcalcifications on imaging studies

cards.excerpt:
Fenestrated proliferation with multiple, round, rigid extracellular lumens with punched out appearance
Neoplastic cells are frequently evenly distributed equidistant and polarized with long axis of cell perpendicular to the central lumen
Trabecular bars comprised of rigid rows of cells with long axes perpendicular or at least not parallel to the long axis of the bar
Roman bridges comprised of curvilinear trabecular bars connecting two portions of the epithelial lining

cards.title: DCIS — Cytology description
cards.excerpt:
Non high grade DCIS: cohesive sheets and aggregates, balls or papillary fragments, mild to variable atypia, some debris, often microcalcifications (Lancet 1995;345:1154, Cancer 2005;105:21)
High grade DCIS: large pleomorphic cells, irregular aggregates and single cells, necrotic debris, individual cell necrosis, microcalcifications (Lancet 1995;345:1154, Cancer 2005;105:21)
Core needle biopsy is preferred to fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) due to the uncertainty in differentiating between in situ and invasive carcinoma by aspiration (Cancer 1998;84:186, Diagn Cytopathol 1993;9:713, Am J Clin Pathol 1989;92:736)
